I would just splurge or save up for AirPods Pro 3 at $199 instead, but if that’s not an option or you just prefer the standard Pods vibe, the decision is perhaps little more of a thing. Woot deal is certainly a notable one. And if you really want that wireless charging case, you are keeping $50 in your pocket over paying full price for the higher-end AirPods 5 here, but you’re also not getting the proper Apple warranty going with the Woot listing. As enticing as 45% off a pair of AirPods is, if I was going with the standard AirPods lineup, I’d go for the proper warranty at $29 more

The iPhone Duo is out there now and Apple specifically recommends you use its 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max to fast charge the new foldable. Just don’t buy one direct, you can get it for less on Amazon right now.

Amazon is offering the official Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max down at $34.99 with free shipping for Prime members or in orders over $35. That’s not a massive deal considering you can score one straight from Apple at $39 any day of the week. But with iPhone Duo out in the wild now and Apple recommending this model for fast charging, we just wanted to make sure folks knew it can be had for less on Amazon.

We did see this one selling for around $27 on Amazon a few times earlier in the year, but it has found new life for some Duo users and it’s hard to say if, or when, it will ever drop any lower in the near future because of it.

It, like the Apple Pencil (USB-C), has started to see a sudden (but not so surprising) surge in popularity among 9to5 readers looking to optimize and elevate the iPhone Duo experience, and you might as well keep a few bucks in your pocket if you’re going to pick one up.

The iPhone Duo is here and if you’re still looking to elevate the experience with Apple Pencil, the only compatible model is the USB-C variant and you can land one at Amazon down at $69 right now. More than a couple staffers have been reporting little to no stock availability at local Apple brick and mortar locations, so we just wanted to touch base to ensure folks know you can easily grab one at Amazon with relatively speedy delivery still and at a lower price – there are even Amazon Resale units at $60 right now.

While the less pricey 16GB/1TB model is still at $200 off, Amazon just brought back its fall Prime Day price on the upgraded 24GB MacBook Air at $200 off as well.

Amazon is once again offering Apple’s 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with 24GB of RAM and the 1TB storage capacity down at $1,599 shipped.

This is a regularly $1,799 configuration that is now $200 off the list price to deliver the lowest we can find online.

We did spot this same deal over the weekend on all four colors, but it quickly disappeared on all of them. While only the Midnight has returned here this afternoon, we are talking about a deal on par with the fall Prime Day price and matching the lowest we have tracked in months.

Unlike the new Apple HomeView, it looks like Amazon is actually going to be holding on to the early pre-order discount on the new Apple TV 4K for now. But you might want to get in there sooner than later before the delivery times slip even further.

Back in September Apple’s Beats brands launched the all-new modular Beats 360 over-ear headphones and today we are catching the very first straight up cash discount on the headphones themselves. Amazon is still also offering the deep 80% launch discount on the interchangeable Cushion Kits.

Amazon is now offering the new black model Beats 360 Over-Ear Headphones down at $329 shipped – the Cloud white colorway is still up at full price.

That’s certainly not a massive discount at just $20 off, but it is the very first chance at any savings at all and we wanted to make sure it was on the radar for the remaining early adopters while the Cushion Kits were still on sale as well.

The Beats 360 feature modular a headband cushion and earpads – you can flip them out/mix and match with any of the official Cushion Kits. These kits carry $50 list prices but Amazon and Beats offered a launch deal on them at 80% off and some of them are still down at just $9.99 apiece.

For a complete rundown on the new Beats 360, head over to our hands-on review right here.

Belkin makes a super clean and minimalist Qi2.2 25W Wireless 2-in-1 foldable charging station and it has now dropped back down to $50 in all three colors.

Amazon is now offering the Belkin Qi2.2 25W UltraCharge 2-in-1 Foldable Charging Station down at $49.99 shipped. This deal price is live on the black, white, and blue colorways.

Regularly $60, deals on this model have largely been hard to come by up until the last month or so. We have seen a couple Prime Day discounts dropping as low as $43, but the deal we have here today is on par with the lowest we have tracked otherwise, coming within $7 of the Amazon all-time low.

As I have said previously, Anker actually makes my favorite foldable MagSafe charging station – the 3-in-1 Prime model you can currently score on sale at $35% off right now. But if you only need a 2-in-1 setup for iPhone and AirPods, this Belkin model is a solid choice and one you can lock in for half the price right now.

The TechPod RePod has to be one of the more compelling ways to repurpose your old Apple Watch. For around $50 with the Amazon deals right now, these things effectively bring your Apple Watch back to life, transforming it into a functional and retro-inspired handheld.

While not all models are discounted on the brand’s Amazon storefront, they do all carry a $60 list and many of them have on page coupons to knock the price down to $50.99 shipped right now. You can also save an extra 5% if you purchase two of them.

There are RePod sizes to support just about all previous-generation Apple Watch models, going right back to Series 4, through the SE models, and right up through to Series 10 and 11. They might be one of, if not, the most interesting way to bring your old Apple wearable back to life I have seen yet.

Just after the reveal of its new AirFly Drive CarPlay and Android Auto wireless adapter for your ride, today Twelve South is ready to upgrade your audio experience in the air. Ready to connect directly to the in-flight entertainment system, the all-new Airfly View adds a built-in display to what was already the one of, if not, the best wireless audio transmitters for your wireless buds and headphones.

Anyone familiar with the previous Airfly transmitters is going to be right at home here again. A staple in packing lists and best of travel accessory guides for years now, Twelve South is bringing its Airfly into the next-generation with the same level of simplicity, but with a new built-in display so you can actually see what’s going on.

Airfly started with one narrow problem: wireless headphones, and the wired jacks still bolted into airplane seatbacks, gym treadmills, and older cars. It has been solving that simply ever since. Airfly View keeps the same simplicity and puts every step on screen.

Airfly View is available starting today in Black and Coastal blue with an included international airline adapter and zippered hard-shell travel case at $79.99.

Twelve South Airfly Drive CarPlay and Android Auto wireless adapter has been one of the more popular tech releases around here over the last month or so, and it’s back. Shipping times started to slip well into December on the popular black model, but Amazon is now listing both it and the white for delivery as soon as next week.

#3388. Brian May Clears Up Queen’s Live Future: ‘I’m on a Break’

Queen‘s Brian May has been spending a lot of time in his studio lately, from his work on the score to June’s Masters of the Universe (out soon on vinyl) to a collaboration with William Shatner. After decades of touring, he’s enjoying time at home, so he’s not anxious to play shows right now — but in a recent Zoom chat with Rolling Stone, he again made it clear that he’s not ruling it out. He also talked about Queen’s scores for Flash Gordon and Highlander, the newly restored Queen Budapest concert film, and more.

The composer Daniel Pemberton, who worked with you on Masters of the Universe, told me you’d sit and think for a while and then play fully formed parts.Yes, that’s the way I tend to be. If I can’t hear it in my head, I can’t play it. ’Cause to me, the guitar is a voice, and if you don’t know what you’re gonna say, it’s pointless opening your mouth, really. You can wheedle, wheedle, wheedle endlessly because things happen when you pick up a guitar, but that’s not really playing the guitar with a purpose. And to me, yes, I always wanna hear it in my head, whether it’s the “Bohemian Rhapsody” solo or it’s a piece of Eternia which we haven’t visited before.

One of my favorite bits on the Masters of the Universe album is the rock version of the Eternia theme that you put together with the Darkness. How did that one happen? I got it into my head that I needed somehow to do the definitive version of what I heard in my head as the Eternia theme. Daniel uses it throughout the movie in different forms. So I wanted to gather them all together and build it up as a rock track, as if it had all come from inside my head instead of his.

So I reconstructed the whole track, pulled everything in that I could find, with the help of Daniel. And then I thought, “Wouldn’t it be great if we could get the Darkness on this as well? It would bring it to life.” And I wanted a bit more vocal anyway, to tell a bit more of the story. The Darkness were already involved in the project — they’d done the end-title theme.So I rang them up. They are really dear friends of mine. Dan came down first, Dan Darkness, as I call him — Dan Hawkins — and he came along and played bass, which I actually wasn’t expecting, but he just instantly said, “Look, I have to play bass on this.” And I said, “Do you think we can talk to your brother about doing some vocals?” And Justin immediately said yes. He was brilliant, Justin, ’cause they were already on tour and halfway around the world, and what he did was take a copy of the track and a little handheld, well, an iPhone I suppose, and just sang into it in his hotel room and sent it over to me, and it was good enough quality for me to put on the track. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

I already wanted Rufus Taylor to play drums. That’s the way I heard it in my head. I think Rufus is just a wonderful drummer, a great musician. I’ve known him since he was knee-high to a grasshopper and he’s a wonderful boy. He really is a beautiful player. So he did that for me, and we recorded it in his dad’s studio, in Roger’s studio. So then I had pretty much all the Darkness on there.

When Queen did Flash Gordon in 1980, that was something genuinely new — a rock band scoring an entire film. The truth is no one had done it, and they told me it couldn’t be done. So yes, you hear freedom, but you hear disbelief really, ’cause they said, “No, you can’t do a score with guitars and rock groups.” And I said, “Look, I can hear it in my head. I believe that we can do it for this, and I think it’ll work atmospherically.”

My favorite story, although it hurts me still, is — well, we saw the rushes, and we all, the four of us in Queen, went away and made little sketches, ideas that we thought we could contribute to the film. I had a few bits and pieces, including the main title “Flash” thing, which I thought would be great to bookend the film and to give it its character. And we reconvened after we’d made these demos of these ideas in Trident Studios with the director Mike Hodges and the producer Dino De Laurentiis. A big, big, big, big, big movie mogul producer. Related Content How Queen's Brian May Recaptured 'Flash Gordon' Magic for 'Masters of the Universe' Watch Queen + Adam Lambert's Last 'We Will Rock You' at Final Show in 2024 Brian May Says Queen Won’t Tour Again: ‘50 Years Is Enough’ 50 Years Ago Today: Queen and the Sex Pistols Play Two Pivotal Shows in England

So he sat there at the control room looking very big and very imposing, and listened to it all, and went, “Yes, yes, yes.” He’s Italian. He doesn’t speak much English, not many words. And finally we got to my title theme, and I played it to him, and he sat there, and he didn’t move a muscle. His face was like stone. And at the end of it he said, “Yes, it’s very good, but it is not for my film.”

That was it. So my heart sank, and Mike Hodges, who’s next to me, whispers in my ear. He said, “Don’t worry, I’ll fix it. It’ll be fine.” And it turned out well, and when we got to the film premiere, Dino came up to me at the gathering after the movie, and he said, “You did a beautiful thing for my movie. I’m very happy.” So that was nice.

What was that about?The problem was that Mike Hodges and Dino had different images in their heads as to what the movie should be. Mike Hodges saw it completely as a retro pastiche, if you like. Kind of tongue-in-cheek comic book epic. Whereas Dino saw it as a very serious major film, in the style of King Kong, something rather serious. He didn’t really see the humor of it and the lovely kind of light touch that was in the original, the Buster Crabbe originals which we’d all seen.

You did Highlander a few years later, and people are more familiar with the songs than the score.Yes, although we did quite a bit of scoring as well, and I personally did a lot of stuff with [composer] Michael Kamen, which I will forever be very proud of. Some of those battle scenes, there’s music behind there which you would never expect, and it was new in those days. I mean, these days people pick up tricks and it’s become commonplace. But in those days, battle scenes were always accompanied by kind of raucous music. Michael Kamen did this beautiful piece for the biggest battle of the movie, which was really low-key and very sad and drawn out, almost like slow motion, and put against the action. It was riveting. It’s the most amazing scene, I think.

So I played on that with him, and he played a few other things. He contributed, although we were sort of the main composers for the movie, what he called the Highlander theme, which not many people know about.And when we did “Who Wants to Live Forever” together, he did the orchestration for that and did a beautiful, monumental job. And if you listen very carefully, you will hear the Highlander theme woven into that.

I spent so many happy hours with Michael. He’s one of these people who can read music if you just put it in front of him, but he can also compose out of nothing. Usually people are one or the other. My dad could play anything by ear. You would sing it to him, and he’d sit down at the piano and play it, but he couldn’t read a note of music. His sister could read any piece of music that you put in front of her, and if you took the music away, she had nothing. I find a lot of musicians fall into one of those categories. I mean, really, I fall into my dad’s category, ’cause my reading of music is very limited. I’m mainly a person who hears things and speaks according to what he hears. But Michael had those two things, and he was wonderful to work with. I really miss having him around. Incredible musician.

The Highlander score has never come out — you released the songs on the Queen album A Kind of Magic instead. You’ve talked about someday putting out the actual score.We did, and yeah, very often that subject’s come up. I would love to do it someday. We skirted around — we avoided doing the soundtrack album, which wasn’t really my decision, but it was a group decision. We thought it would be better to have a Queen album out there rather than a soundtrack album. But yes, there’s a lot of lovely stuff which I would love to see on a CD sometime. Do they still have CDs?

They’re on a bit of an upswing, actually. Kids are buying them to collect, some without owning a CD player.It’s nice to have something that you can touch and feel and hold.

So people were under the impression recently that you swore off touring with Queen. Oh, yeah, I got kind of misinterpreted, slightly misquoted there. I never said we’ll never tour again. I don’t know how I could ever say that. I couldn’t.

I feel like I’m on a break, and I’m enjoying my break, and I’m getting to do all the things which I dreamed of doing when there was no time all those years on the road. So I’m getting to see my kids, I’m getting to see my grandchildren, getting to do a lot of projects on the side which I’ve dreamed of doing. I get to do more astrophysics. I get to do more animal welfare and animal campaigning work. And all round, it’s been a good decision for me so far.

Maybe one day I’m gonna wake up and think, “Ah, maybe we should get out on the road.” But I don’t think I will be committing to nine-month-long tours again. I think I’ll be happy just doing — I mean, at the moment I get to play just when I want to, which is not a bad deal really. I just played with Andrea Bocelli at the Starmus Festival. It’s great fun. It’s a different kind of challenge altogether. And I played with Benson Boone, which I really enjoyed, and I get to do loads of stuff in the studio.

What about the Sphere? You were fairly warm on that idea when we last spoke.Yeah, I don’t know what to tell you about that. I don’t even know where we are on that. I really don’t. Things change so fast.

I’m still very much caught up with the idea of this 360-degree surround environment for music, and particularly for us in some kind of retrospective. It wouldn’t be like the ABBA thing. Everybody says, “Oh, you’re gonna do what ABBA did.” But no, it would be something different from that, because we have a different history and a different path or whatever. And I still have a template in my head of what we could do, but I don’t think we’re progressing very fast on it for various other reasons. So you’re kind of getting “I don’t know” from me.

You told me you’d played around in the studio with Adam Lambert to try some new Queen music. Is that still a possibility?Well, it was a long time ago. That was very early in the relationship. We did try it once. I think it was in Nashville. Went in for a night, and it seemed to be an interesting avenue, but we didn’t really feel it was quite happening, and we never returned. That’s all I can tell you.

Are you still in touch with Adam? If there’s a project, is he the singer, or is that open too?We’re in touch. I went to see him when he came over. I enjoyed seeing his show when he was over here at the Roundhouse. We haven’t talked about doing anything. I suppose I’m not in that place, really. I don’t want to be a touring animal at this point, and I don’t want to retrace those steps. Again, I can’t say never. How could you ever? So yeah, it’s a sort of open question[s].

You said you’ve been doing a lot in the studio instead. What’s come out of that?I love taking up a challenge. I like being offered a gig in the studio, in a sense. So I did this track with William Shatner, which I think is stupendous. I just love it. You know, the guy’s 95 and he’s decided to make a heavy metal album, and I was very happy to contribute to that track, which I think is actually very significant. It’s based on Dylan Thomas. And it’s very well done, I think. So I kind of put my producer’s hat on as well, and decided to do a few things with it.

But that’s a thrill. I’ve worked with my grandson. We have a new track, which is, I think, coming out in a couple of months’ time. That’s an interesting track, completely new, and he plays most of the guitar, to be honest, which is great. I have a grandson who can play guitar, and write songs, and be in a group. Who would have thought?

And Graham Bonnet came with a track which is a dedication to Rory Gallagher, a great hero of mine, so we did it together. Very happy with that. I’ve just seen the first cut of the little video that we’ve been putting together about that. Very satisfying for me, ’cause Rory was such a massive influence on me. And as the song said, really nobody played anything in memory of him, so now they have. This is a commemorative track to him.

Who else?I’m also working with a guy called Noel Fitzpatrick. I don’t know if you know him, but he is the Supervet on TV. He’s the guy who can repair animals that nobody else can fix. And he can do things with dogs and cats which people can’t even do with humans, like growing new limbs. It’s quite incredible. He’s become a very dear friend of mine, and his whole mission in life is to bring medicine together, animal medicine and human medicine together, rather than animals being experimented on in order to make medicine for humans. He says everything should march forward together. We are all basically one species when it comes down to it. So he’s a great guy to work with. We have a track which we’ve been working on, which kind of says all this.

So what does he do musically?He writes most of the lyrics — I think probably all of the lyrics. He has a band. And he plays guitar. Now, he took up guitar about probably 18 months ago, and I gave him one of my guitars to encourage him. And we spent some time together, and I had no idea that he would really take it that seriously. I mean, he’s one of the world’s greatest veterinary surgeons, but he’s up between three and four AM practicing every night, and he now is a guitarist. So they do some gigs, and they’ve written this bunch of songs, and I was very drawn to this particular one, which I’ve now played on, and I’ve actually sung it as well now, as tends to happen sometimes.

The restored Queen Budapest film is out. What did seeing it bring back?What the hell do I say about this? You open that box, and there we were in this kind of touring bubble, and the ever-increasing position of Queen in the world, and we’re doing our first ever stadium tour. We’re kind of flying high, and Freddie’s in wonderful form physically and mentally. We’ve just done Wembley Stadium, two nights, packed, sold out, wonderful, a year after Live Aid, when we’d sort of made our first appearance at Wembley Stadium. We’re now back out in Europe, in Budapest, behind the Iron Curtain, where no rock group has ever been able to play, and it’s a monumental moment. It really is.

So to go back into that — and it was well filmed, very well documented by the top cinematographers of the time, who happened to be pretty much all Hungarian. And it was beautifully edited, and they filmed us in the city. There’s all sorts of little insights into what we were doing offstage as well as onstage, and I think it’s beautiful, and it was great to be able to restore it sound-wise and visual-wise. The wonderful people in New Zealand did the restoration of the visuals, the people who do Lord of the Rings and stuff. And we did the sound restoration, and it’s beautiful. Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Martha Stewart 'Distressed' by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume My Chemical Romance Tops the Billboard 200 With 20-Year-Old Album Harry Styles Ended His Historic Madison Square Garden Run — And This Song Captured It All

Roger and I went to the premiere, as it were, the first showing in the IMAX, and somebody asked Roger how he felt, and he said, “I feel exhausted.” And that’s exactly how you feel — because you get emotionally dragged through that whole thing. It’s almost like you’re there and you’re still worried about, did you make a mistake or did that sound right, and you’re back in all those personal issues that you had at the time. It is an exhausting experience for us to look at it.

But I feel proud. Detaching yourself, I think that it’s a good band, very well in touch with each other, very well-oiled machine, and it’s a great moment. I’m glad it was captured.

#3385. Juan Atkins, Techno Music Pioneer, Dead at 64

Juan Atkins, the originator of techno music and a founding member of the electronic music group Cybotron, has died at the age of 64.

Atkins’ talent agency Greensmith Artists confirmed the DJ and producer’s death on social media. Resident Advisor reports that Atkins was found unresponsive in his hotel room prior to his performance Saturday in Mexico City. Atkins was declared dead at the hospital soon after.

Born in the Motor City and raised in nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins became synonymous with techno music alongside fellow classmates Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May, the “Belleville Three” who are credited as the architects of Detroit Techno, which fused the house music playing in Chicago and the electronic music of bands like Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra.

After initially first performing as a DJ, Atkins formed the electronic music group Cybotron with college classmate Rik Davis in 1980. The duo released one album together, the influential 1983 LP Enter, before splitting up in 1985.

Atkins next formed his own record label, Metroplex, as well as began recording under the moniker Model 500. It was under that name that Atkins released his 1985 single “No UFO’s,” a track credited with bringing Detroit techno across the Atlantic when it inspired the U.K. compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit.

“Juan Atkins invented techno, full stop — he conceived it and named it — and one of its many aspects that he pioneered was the use of multiple aliases for different types of work,” Rolling Stone wrote in 2025 when “No UFO’s” landed on our list of the 200 Greatest Dance Songs of All Time.

“Lush and insistent, ‘No UFO’s,’ the first Model 500 12-inch, set the template for the Detroit approach. ‘They make these synthesizers and keyboards with functions that allow you to get as close to a human feel as they possibly can,'” Atkins said in 1997. “‘I think this is the beauty of Detroit, we were able to put that emotion into our music.'” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“The term ‘techno’ got exploited. I mean, even now, techno in Germany is different from techno in Spain. Here in Detroit everybody loved the music,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “Nobody knew that it was techno music. Especially the Black kids in Detroit. All they knew was that this was a new sound. And whatever it was, whatever the frequency makeup was, it just pushed a button somewhere. When it got to Europe, Europe had to give it some kind of title.”

Atkins continued to record under the Model 500 moniker over the next three decades, as well as the aliases Infiniti (for his minimalist techno work, highlighted on the 1998 album Skynet), Audio Tech, and his own name.

Atkins also released albums with fellow electronic music artist like Moritz von Oswald (as Borderland) and toured with May and Saunderson as The Belleville Three in the 2010s.

“Heartbreaking news today. My brother Juan Atkins has passed away,” Saunderson wrote on social media Sunday. “Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included. I’ll never forget how he showed me how to finish my first record, Triangle of Love. That meant a lot to me then, and it still does today.” Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Martha Stewart 'Distressed' by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume My Chemical Romance Tops the Billboard 200 With 20-Year-Old Album Harry Styles Ended His Historic Madison Square Garden Run — And This Song Captured It All

Saunderson continued, “We shared a journey that changed music forever, and I’ll always be grateful for his friendship, guidance and everything he gave to our scene.”

“A great DJ is a leader. A mediocre DJ is a follower,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “That’s what I try in DJ’ing and making music and presenting music. The public attention span is pretty short, and people are always interested in what’s next. Not so much what happened yesterday. Not so much what’s happening right now. But what’s next?”

#3383. Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac

Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.

Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…

The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.

It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.

John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:

We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL

Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro.

Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.

Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here. The new machines are also available on Amazon.

Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini, M6 iMac, and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration.

The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos. We’re so back. pic.twitter.com/Ce6G8EIVQF

The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.

Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.

The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.

Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

I honestly think this is a downgrade. Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar? It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it. Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook. What’s the actual point?

If it supported the Apple Pencil, I could understand the appeal, especially for designers. But without it, I honestly don’t see much use for it. Maybe I’m wrong, but I’ve used touchscreen Windows laptops before, and I never really found it useful.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction. Apple needs a better marketing team that understands what people actually want, rather than adding a touchscreen that, in my opinion, offers very little practical use.

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.

Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.

You can find Apple’s press release for the new machines here. All configurations are available to order from Amazon.

#3382. Sean 'Diddy' Comb's New Prison Release Date Revealed

Sean "Diddy" Combs' prison release date has been shifting for months --- and now his latest walk-out date has been moved up more than 3 weeks, TMZ has learned.

The federal Bureau of Prisons says Diddy will now be a free man on February 6, 2028, instead of March 2, 2028, which was his projected release date last month. Previous release dates also included January 21, February 5, and February 20.

This is great news for Diddy after all of his troubles at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey, leading to his recent transfer to FCI Allenwood in Pennsylvania.

While he was at Fort Dix, Diddy was tossed in solitary confinement for allegedly violating the rules by getting into fights and using contraband cellphones. NBC News also reported that Diddy enjoyed VIP treatment at Fort Dix because he paid other inmates to give him massages, cook his meals, and do his chores.

Diddy was found guilty by a trial jury in 2025 on two counts of the Mann Act -- transporting people across state lines for prostitution. Diddy was acquitted on the more serious charges of racketeering and sex trafficking. A judge sentenced Diddy to 50 months in federal prison on the lesser charges.

The Netflix slate for the week ahead has been confirmed, and as November gets underway, Netflix isn’t waiting any longer to bring the festive cheer. Over the next seven days, there will be plenty to watch on the world’s biggest streaming service, so I’m picking out the highlights.

#3377. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3371. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3370. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference

Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR this week (pre-order here), which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has an all-new industrial design. It’s the first design overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

You still get a 14.2-inch regardless of whether you choose PROLED XDR or not. On the 16-inch model, PROLED XDR is 16.3 inches, slightly larger than the standard 16.2-inch.

Apple’s new design is a bit sleeker and significantly lighter-weight. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the lid that was an iconic element in previous generations. Additionally, the PROLED XDR has a newly designed hinge that provides greater stability.

Here’s a breakdown of how each model compares in size and weight:

As the numbers show, the overall size difference is fairly minor, but the reduced weight should be obvious to anyone who upgrades.

The new MacBook Pro’s display technology is so important, Apple put it in the branding. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR features a tandem OLED that Apple says is “the world’s best laptop display.”

Again, it’s available in 14.2-inch or 16.3-inch sizes that are nearly identical to the standard MacBook Pro.

The PROLED XDR display is touch-enabled, with macOS 27 introducing a variety of optimizations for touch input. So if you want a touchscreen on your Mac, that’s a big advantage.

Tandem OLED means you’ll get deeper blacks, true-to-life color, and also a new max peak brightness of 2,000 nits (up from 1,600). And Adobe RGB is now supported, along with a host of industry-standard reference modes.

There’s also a Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro. It replaces the notch and serves as the home to software features like Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Apple is using the exact same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in its two MacBook Pros, so performance should in theory be the same across models.

That said, real-world testing will reveal whether the new MacBook Pro design has an impact on sustained performance—for better or worse.

Memory options are also identical with the PROLED XDR model and standard MacBook Pro. That means:

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR largely retains the same storage options as the standard MacBook Pro, with one exception.

The only change here is that there’s now a high-end 16TB option when you choose M5 Max. Previously, 8TB was the most storage available in any MacBook Pro.

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers identical battery life and fast charging features as the standard MacBook Pro. That means:

All MacBook Pro models can fast charge up to 50 percent battery in 30 minutes.

Apple’s MacBook Pro models all feature the same 12MP Center Stage camera with support for Desk View, 1080p HD video recording, and an advanced image signal processor with computational video.

However, because of touchscreen support, the PROLED XDR model adds one new feature: Advanced Video Stabilization.

Essentially, this exists so that if you’re touching your display during a video call, it won’t have an impact on your camera feed.

The MacBook Pro PROLED XDR features largely the same speaker system as the standard model, but with a pair of key upgrades. Per Apple Newsroom:

The industry-leading six-speaker audio system in the new MacBook Pro features an all-new woofer design that provides 50 percent deeper bass and all-new tweeters that shape sound dispersion for remarkable clarity…And for the first time, dedicated audio tuning for closed-lid use delivers exceptional sound quality when MacBook Pro is connected to an external display, so users can enjoy a premium audio experience however they work.

Apple clearly learned from past mistakes of removing ports from pro users. With the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, you get all the same ports as on the standard MacBook Pro. Ports include:

One upgrade that will benefit some users is that Genlock is now supported by the Thunderbolt 5 ports as well.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. That’s a $400 premium over the standard MacBook Pro.

Apple’s standard MacBook Pro starts at $2,499 for the 14-inch size and $2,999 for the larger 16-inch.

Warm fuzzies for the return of the glowing Apple logo but I won't need the other features so it's not worth the extra $400 to me.

Overall, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers a lot of upgrades over the standard model, but with the same basic performance and battery life. If you want a better display, touch support, a Dynamic Island, and various other smaller improvements, PROLED XDR is the way to go.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display here for launch-day delivery.

#3369. My Chemical Romance Tops the Billboard 200 With 20-Year-Old Album

Twenty years after The Black Parade, My Chemical Romance have carried on with the album all the way to the top of the Billboard 200 chart. The 2006 LP’s anniversary reissue The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition) nabbed the top slot, marking the rock band’s first Number One album in their nearly 25 years as a band.

The deluxe reissue sold 78,000 equivalent album units across over 20 formats and variants combined to take the top spot, Billboard reports.

Released in 2006, The Black Parade saw the emo band expand their sound on their third album with a fully-fledged rock opera in the vein of Queen that yielded Top Ten hit “Welcome to the Black Parade.” The album debuted at Number Two on the albums chart in 2006 upon the album’s release. In the two decades since then, The Black Parade has become a seminal rock record of the 21st century.

My Chemical Romance celebrated the album’s 20th anniversary with a full reissue The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Edition) on Oct. 23. The physical sales propelled the album to the top of the charts. On Friday, the band scored their first Number One on the U.K.’s official album chart. Though the band ran into a bit of legal trouble with the Dallas Cowboys cheerleading team, the tour has been a career-defining feat. Last year, they performed at their hometown stadium in New Jersey and even took the show to London’s Wembley Stadium for two sold-out nights. The band’s feat on the chart not only cements The Black Parade as a timeless record, it also reinforces My Chemical Romance’s status as rock icons — and their unstoppable comeback.

The co-pilot who died in a horrific private jet crash in Florida has been identified as a 20-year-old woman who earned her pilot's license before graduating high school.

As for the deadly crash ... the jet was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it suddenly went into a terrifying nosedive, with flight data showing it was dropping more than 20,000 feet per minute.

The plane slammed into the ground near a mobile home park, erupting into a massive fireball and killing all nine people aboard.

I'm Erin, and welcome to The Coffee Lab Episode 24, the series where we forget coffee snobbery. The Coffee Lab is all about making coffee fun. Join me as I help you kickstart your coffee journey!

Controversial opinion incoming, but if you don't have an espresso machine, you can still make great-tasting coffee at home. Some coffee snobs will disagree, and that's fine, but this recipe isn't for them. This is for the I-love-coffee-but-I-can't-afford-a-machine crowd. I see you! I'm here for you!

I used to be a Starbucks barista, so the amount of PSLs I've made is off the charts. Although Starbucks keeps its PSL sauce recipe pretty secret, you can get copycat-ish syrups everywhere online, so you can easily make the fall favorite at home. To make it even more Starbucks-y, just add a touch of condensed milk to the pumpkin syrup. For this recipe, I used Monin Pumpkin Spice syrup ($10 on Amazon), but you can use any you like.

The Coffee Lab is all about making coffee fun and accessible, so let's demystify the ubiquitous fall drink! It's no-machine PSL time.

I used Nescafé Instant Espresso ($10 at Amazon) for this recipe, but you can use anything you like. Add one or two teaspoons, depending on strength preference, and a dash — about one ounce — of hot water to mix.

Didn't I say this was easy? Now combine your pumpkin spice syrup (remember, condensed milk and orange food coloring if you want it truly Starbucks-y), and instant espresso. Mix, and you're done!

You can prepare your milk in multiple ways. Either simply heat it up in the microwave (which is what I did for this recipe), or you can use a milk frother. I have the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro 2 ($159) and the Subminimal Nanofoamer Go ($34). The moral of the story is to use whatever you have!

And you're done. I said this was easy, didn't I?

You can add whipped cream or nutmeg on top if you want to make it even fancier.

I'm not going to lie: this will not fool any PSL diehards. You can tell it's not Starbucks from just looking at it — Starbucks PSLs are bright orange. However, for a fraction of the cost, and without requiring you to fork out on an espresso machine, I'm extremely happy drinking my Pumpkin Spice Faux-tte all fall long.

#3365. Harry Styles Ended His Historic Madison Square Garden Run — And This Song Captured It All

Each night during his 30-show run at Madison Square Garden, Harry Styles posed the same string of questions to his audience through “Season 2 Weight Loss,” from his fourth album Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally: “Do you love me now? Do you? Do you? Do I let you down?”

The song occupies one of the darkest moments in the set, and not just for its anxious interrogations — beyond red and blue strobes, the stage is largely devoid of light throughout its four-minute duration. It also finds Styles at this most physically distant. He spends almost the entirety of the performance in the center of the stage, away from the perimeter he otherwise treats as a combination dancefloor-treadmill-playground. And yet, it’s the most illuminating part of the show.

Styles mirrors the pounding percussion of the song with full-bodied thrashing. He stumbles frantically, but never falls. In front of 20,000 people, he takes “dance like no one’s watching” to the extreme, mostly because he knows everyone is. It’s fitting for a record so preoccupied with the tension of performance, not solely from the perspective of an artist, but a person who wants so badly to show up without dissolving the dissonance between who they are and who people believe them to be. In that regard, “Season 2 Weight Loss” is perhaps the most important song Styles has ever released.

Styles has spoken before about carrying the weight of pressure and emotional expectations that often compound what he might already be feeling. It’s an extension of the central conflict within “Season 2 Weight Loss,” in that particular moment where he sings, “It’s kind of sad, but there’s something I know/Too many things for you to analyze.” He seems to be thinking, perhaps now more than ever, about what pieces of himself shape how we understand, or in some cases misunderstand, who he is. It’s become more important as he continues to reconfigure his relationship with stardom.

Styles’ questions about devotion and doubt landed differently on Saturday, which marked the last show of the residency after 10 weeks. Madison Square Garden is the smallest room he’ll play on the Together, Together tour, which is otherwise solely booked in stadiums with three and four times the capacity. An audience of this size is considered an intimate one for him now. Watching him pull an enclosed room into his dizzying trance one last time brought an added urgency to the song — it even transcended the fact that he walked onto the stage dressed as a rat, then changed into a shirt that read, “I Am A Rat.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

During the penultimate residency show, Styles recreated the outfit he wore to his audition for The X Factor when he was 16 years old, which was 16 years ago. He did so surrounded by his band members, who were dressed as different versions of him from throughout his career. Styles’ existentialism rubbed off on the fans, who anxiously awaited what he might have in store for the final night — what he might say, what he might sing, how he might say goodbye to this moment.

“I’m going to venture back to the safety of my mic stand because I’m feeling vulnerable and I’m not sure what to do with my hands,” Styles said after New York Knicks point guard Jalen Brunson presented him with a banner commemorating his 30-night run on Saturday night. The praise from the crowd washed over Styles as he cried. He prolonged the night for as long as he reasonably could, closing out the show with an extended dance mix of “Aperture,” during which he danced around the stage while scarfing down pizza slices. The moment felt endless. If only it could have been.

Back in September, Styles wrote a letter to his fans that sent them into crisis mode. “Being an artist is the only life I’ve ever known really, I have been doing this since I was 16 years old, and I feel like the luckiest person in the world to still be sharing these moments with you,” he said, noting he would be expanding the Together, Together tour into next year. “After that, I don’t know what comes next for me, but I know that I’m excited to find out.” Fans poured over every word and every possible interpretation seemed to lead back to the same thing. Related Content Harry Styles Honored by Jalen Brunson at Madison Square Garden, Receives 30 Nights Banner Harryween Is Back From Dead: Harry Styles Dons 'X Factor' Outfit for Stevie Wonder Cover Manhattan Will Celebrate Harry Styles Appreciation Day Harry Styles Performs ‘Ever Since New York’ During Final Week of Madison Square Garden Residency

“If I go away, and grow, and change my relationship with this idea of feeling like I have to show up as this version of myself — will you take me as that?” Styles said in an interview with Zane Lowe. “Or are you taking me because I show up as this version of myself that you’ve desired from me in some way?” This tension has always existed for Styles, but the song revels in the confidence of having built such a strong connection to his audience that he can deploy this level of communication, even when it feels slightly anxious and confrontational, without fracturing that.

His last tour, Love on Tour, may have cemented this honest relationship as a possibility for him. “I think it was a realization that these shows felt like a culmination of so many people’s support,” Styles recently told Thom Yorke as part of Rolling Stone’s Musicians on Musicians. He was talking about the overwhelming finale of the tour, which ran for 169 shows across nearly two years. “I felt supported, in a way that’s more than like, ‘We’re here because we want to hear this song that you’ve done.’ It just felt like, ‘We’re here because we believe in what you’re doing.’ That’s why I found it so emotional.”

When he retreats for long stretches of time, Styles returns with albums that are reflective of the self-interrogation he completed during those periods. Now, all he’s asking is for everyone else to do the same — sit with that discomfort and what it reveals when allowed to settle. “You’ve got to sit yourself down sometimes,” he sings. When he’s standing in the center of the stage, singing these words and pleading for answers, it’s when Styles feels the closest. “Season 2 Weight Loss” isn’t as overtly emotional as something like “Carla’s Song,” which he reconfigured as a beautiful piano ballad for the New York run, but it is the most vulnerable moment in the show.

Styles spoke each night during the residency about having had the honor of performing at the Garden for the first time at 18 years old. He’s spent nearly half of his life being welcomed into that room with open arms, first with One Direction, then over and over again on his own. And yet in all those years, Styles has never put on a show as absorbing and certain as the Together, Together set he brought to New York. His other tours, in support of his first three studio albums, felt like watching someone become who they were always meant to be.  Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Martha Stewart 'Distressed' by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume My Chemical Romance Tops the Billboard 200 With 20-Year-Old Album Harry Styles Ended His Historic Madison Square Garden Run — And This Song Captured It All

There was an evident effort on display in those days — the custom couture suits on the first tour, the outsized showmanship on the second, his solo rendition of “What Makes You Beautiful” across them both. Styles was in the beginning stages of building his legacy in a way that felt lucky to witness in real-time. This time was different. Now, he’s living in it. Walking out of Madison Square Garden on Saturday, it was overwhelmingly clear this show wasn’t just about watching something special take shape. It reaped the rewards of leading with what felt most inarguably true — that none of us are exempt from the changes time brings, but we are responsible for how we spend it.

If we choose to spend that time together, in rooms like these, it’s worth following the advice Styles offers on “Season 2 Weight Loss”: “Let light come in once in a while.”

#3364. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete excels on hard floors with its side-sweeping arms, mapping navigation, low-maintenance base station, user-friendly app, and stylish design. However, like many robot vacuums, its carpet performance is disappointing.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When deciding on the best robot vacuum for your home, it can seem like the choices are endless. But there are some brands that perform better than others. Dreame consistently impresses me, and the X50 Ultra Complete is no exception.

It has impressive performance on hard floors and a user-friendly app to organize cleaning routines. The design is great, and the base station makes it easy to maintain. Mapping is efficient, and navigation is top-notch.

It’s worth noting that carpet performance isn’t the best, and the suction power isn’t as strong as other flagship models from Dreame. To find out more, keep reading this full Dreame X50 Ultra Complete review.

The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete is available in the U.S. for $1,099 from Amazon, or from Amazon U.K. for £699. The robot vacuum comes in black or white, so you can select the one that best suits your home.

Though the X50 is a flagship model from Dreame, the company released the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete earlier this year, which costs $1,699 and offers more advanced features. The new model has up to 42,000Pa suction, which is more than double that of the X50, and more advanced object avoidance and detection. I gave the X60 a five-star review as it really blew me away, so if you have an extra $600 to spend on your robovac, it’s worth getting the upgraded model.

The MOVA V70 is the same price as the X50 Ultra Complete and has a higher maximum suction power of 42,000Pa. MOVA is part of the same family as Dreame, so the performance is to a very high standard. The MOVA is the winner here for me since the features are slightly more advanced.

Another option with a slightly higher suction power than the X50 Ultra Complete is the Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for $799. This robovac has 25,000Pa of suction and 65 days of self-maintenance, but it’s a lot smaller than the Dreame.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Like most products from Dreame, the X50 Ultra Complete looks more like a piece of home decor than a home appliance. The base station measures 23.2 x 18 x 13.4 inches, so it’s pretty big. But if you have the space, the design helps it blend in.

The base station houses a clean and dirty water tank to refill the robot for mopping, and a large dustbin. The robovac empties after every use.

The robot is around the same size as most other robot vacuums. At 13.8 x 13.8 x 4.4 inches, it can easily fit under furniture in my home and maneuver between chairs at the dining table. The Pro Leap system helps the robot climb over boundaries with two small arms that extend on the underside. This is useful if you have small steps between rooms.

A 360º scanning sensor rises from the top of the robot to map surroundings to avoid spinning when finding its position. The sensor lowers when the robot moves beneath furniture.

The mop pads on the robot are circular, which I prefer to the roller mop present on the Roomba Max 775 Combo. I think the mop’s circular shape does a better job of cleaning and getting into room edges.

I’ve used the Dreame app when testing other robot vacuums from the brand, and it’s still one of my favorites. Creating an account is quick and easy, and you can program cleaning schedules and adjust the settings.

The interface is easy to digest, and all the settings you can change on the device are clearly set out. If you’re not already familiar with the Dreame app, that’s not a problem since you get a walkthrough when you first download the app. I find this helpful as a little refresher for each new product I test, as sometimes these controls can change.

Mapping with the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete is easy. It took around five minutes to map four rooms, and this process was so fast because of the 360º scanner on top. The map is created using LiDAR.

It displays accurate boundaries. It even identified the type of floor and any obstacles on the floor, including shoes and loose wires from other devices.

Like most robot vacuums, the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete performed best on hard floors. I was also impressed by the vacuum’s performance on carpet, considering it only has 20,000Pa of suction. However, there are other vacuums with higher suction that will be much better if you have pets.

tested how well the Dreame C50 Ultra Complete worked while vacuuming, first by testing on carpet and then on hard floor. I followed our usual standardized lab testing criteria at home. While it did a decent job on the hard floors, the carpet performance was more disappointing.

The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete did a good job of picking up most of what I threw at it, and the side-sweeping arm guided the debris right into its path.

The vacuum manages to pick up 80-90% of all debris on the floor during testing, which is quite impressive at 20,000Pa. It took a while to pick up the hair, as the brush moved it around the floor a little, getting it caught in the roller.

As you can see from the results below, the performance on carpet wasn’t as good, but this is a common theme with most robot vacuums. It particularly struggled with picking up flax seeds jumping around the carpet due to vibrations.

However, if you have pets at home, I would recommend the newer version, the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete, as the higher suction power copes better with pet hair.

To evaluate the mopping capabilities of the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete, I put ketchup, mayonnaise and soy sauce on my kitchen floor. I let these dry for a while before creating a mopping route for the robovac to get cleaning.

It did a good job of clearing up all of the mess, and there wasn’t any residue left on the floor afterwards.

The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete can self-empty for up to 100 days, depending on usage in your home. Since the base station has hot water to wash the mop pads along with a heated air cycle, you don’t need to wash the mops yourself, which makes maintenance very easy.

The side brushes will experience wear and tear after some time, and Dreame recommend you should replace them every three to six months to ensure they continue sweeping to the best of their ability.

The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete is a great choice for homes with hard floors and minimal carpet. It picks up most debris on hard floors with help from the side-sweeping arms, and has great navigation from mapping to help it clean every corner of the room. The base station makes the robovac easy to maintain, and the user-friendly app makes it easy to program and track cleaning routines. The cherry on top is the design that makes the base look like a piece of home decor.

Unfortunately, the X50 Ultra Complete doesn’t perform the best on carpets, but I’ve come to expect that with robot vacuum cleaners.

I think this is a perfectly good robot vacuum, but I’d recommend buying the newer flagship model, the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete, for even more suction power.
