#3225. OpenAI’s Lehane likens backing a data centre ban to the 2002 Iraq vote

The Chris Lehane memo lands a day before the midterms, as OpenAI readies a push for AI ‘speed limits’. It also wants data centres renamed ‘compute campuses’.

Chris Lehane, now OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in September 2023.

AI will be the number-one issue of the 2028 US presidential election, says Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer. His memo, titled “2028: The AI Election”, sets out five questions he says candidates must answer to build an AI agenda.

Politico published the Chris Lehane memo in full on Monday, a day before the US midterm elections.

Lehane writes that 2028 has echoes of 1932, the last peacetime presidential race held during a change on this scale. Franklin D. Roosevelt won it, and his New Deal reimagined the social contract.

A candidate who sets out a “compelling third path” will have a chance to define a new contract, Lehane writes. That path runs between those who would let AI advance “without speed limits” and those who would keep control over the technology “in the hands of a self-appointed elite”.

By early October, one in five ads by Democratic candidates or groups mentioned data centres, according to the memo. Of the Democratic ads that criticised data centres in October, the vast majority ran in a handful of states, the memo says. They were mainly Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas, where the sites are being planned and built.

At an early 2028 Democratic event, Lehane writes, candidates could be asked to raise their hands to back a moratorium on data centres. Six months later, the US could lose its AI lead to China for lack of computing power, he adds.

“This could well be the 2028 version of the 2002 vote to go to war in Iraq,” Lehane wrote.

He also writes that OpenAI’s analysts found likely Chinese Communist Party influence operations in the US. They posted social media comments and images claiming that AI buildouts were raising household electricity bills, according to the memo.

The memo cites polling that Lehane says he has seen or run himself. In his own polling, voters prefer a candidate who leads their party in shaping AI policy over one who follows it, by 25 points. Some 66% support continued AI development, including 53% who want stronger safeguards, while 24% favour a pause.

The five questions cover safety and human control, taxes, children and jobs, affordability, and the race with China. On safety, Lehane writes that “AI is a machine, not a person”. He calls for enforceable safety standards, independent assessments and the power to restrict or shut down systems when needed.

On jobs, he writes that OpenAI’s compute campus in Piketon, Ohio alone will need 25,000 skilled tradespeople.

OpenAI will launch a policy push right after Tuesday’s vote, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen reported for Axios on Sunday. It starts in the lame-duck session of Congress, which opens on 9 November.

OpenAI will unveil new ideas for mandatory safeguards on the most powerful AI systems, which it calls “speed limits”, Axios reported. In September, OpenAI asked Congress for national safety rules. It will also offer community deals for new data centres. And it will propose state laws that give residents a say in how the sites get built.

“You’re going to see us talk more and more about the concept of speed limits,” Lehane told Axios.

OpenAI also wants its data centres called “compute campuses”. A spokesperson confirmed the new name to Business Insider.

“Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we’re building for AI,” the spokesperson said.

Last week, TNW reported that voters in Iowa and Ohio back AI safety measures over winning the AI race. Lehane’s memo itself says there was “little room to be ‘for’ AI infrastructure” in the 2026 campaigns.

For the midterms, OpenAI and Anthropic will each run a “war room”, Ashley Gold reported for Semafor. Their job is to keep election information on the two companies’ platforms accurate. It is a first for both.

#3224. Apple Maps begins blurring NASA, Space Force, and Air Force bases

You’re not a real space or aviation nerd unless you’ve taken to a map service and zoomed on the historic NASA launch pads or your local Air Force Bases, just for fun, you know? However, a recent change to Apple Maps now has some of those locations blurred from view, blocking anyone from seeing fighters on tarmacs or rockets on launch pads.

It probably makes sense as a reasonable security measure, why should some of the most sensitive locations to the United States be easily seen from commercial services on anyone’s phone?

Not every base we’ve checked has been blurred. Some rather large US Navy installations like Pearl Harbor, Norfolk, and Naval Station Great Lakes are left unburied. As a Wisconsin resident, I checked my local Air National Guard bases, those two have been left clear to see.

What we have discovered are now blurred are a lot of NASA and US Space Force locations, including Wallops Flight Facility, Virginia, Stennis Space Center, Mississippi, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and Vandenberg Space Force Base, California.

This change looks to have been rather recent, with no announcement by Apple for the change. On the contrary, Google Maps, has not blurred any of these military locations. It is presumed that Apple will continue to role out blurred map changes to more bases in the future.

Apple’s choice for which locations to blur first is interesting. Whiteman Air Force Base, the location of the bulk of the Air Force’s B2 stealth bombers, capable of carrying nuclear weapons, is logically blurred from view. Ellsworth Air Force Base, one of two state-side homes of the B-1B stealth bomber, both nuclear capable and can carry the most payload than any other US bomber, is also blurred. However, Dyess Air Force Base, the second home of the B-1B and Barksdale, home of the vast majority of the 74 year old and still kicking B-52s, are not blurred.

It’s no surprise that Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (featured image), is parent base Patricks Space Force Base, and Vandenberg Space Force Base are all blurred. These locations are home to the bulk of military owned launch pads and house some of the world’s most advanced and secretive satellites ever built.

But no need to worry too much, for now it seems that Kennedy Space Center and its historic launch pads, LC-39A and LC-39B, is not blurred. That doesn’t mean NASA isn’t on the list, Wallops Flight Facility, a primarily civil research focused air field owned by NASA is blurred, but it’s launch pads, also owned by NASA, are not.

Finally, two other locations that may be top on the list of online map explorers, Groom Lake (Area 51) and the Los Alamos National Laboratory and also now blurred.

Without a formal announcement from Apple, we aren’t sure how quickly the company plans to blur over future bases; and if it’s just highly sensitive facilities or if all government locations are on the list to be blurred.

Some questions that I now have are how navigation works on these blurred bases. Does Apple CarPlay work still? Or if military personnel and civilians working at these bases need to find a new service for on base navigation needs.

Seth Kurkowski covers launches and general space news for Space Explored. He has been following launches from Florida since 2018.
